q_f13d366a2267.explanation: AWS CloudFormation provisions infrastructure from templates, and the same template can be deployed as stacks in multiple Regions (for example with StackSets), which fits IaC at scale.

optionNotes.A: CloudWatch monitors metrics, logs, and alarms; it does not deploy infrastructure from code.
optionNotes.B: AWS Config records and evaluates resource configurations; it does not provision stacks.
optionNotes.C: Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations; it does not deploy infrastructure.
optionNotes.D: CloudFormation is the IaC service that creates and manages resources from templates, including repeatable deployments across Regions.

q_f6b170c8b3e8.explanation: AWS CloudTrail records API calls and account activity, including who made the call and when, so it fits tracking API activity against AWS resources.

optionNotes.A: CloudWatch collects performance metrics and logs, not a record of who made API calls.
optionNotes.B: Amazon Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities; it does not track API activity.
optionNotes.C: CloudTrail logs API calls made in the account, which is exactly the tracking requirement.
optionNotes.D: IAM controls who can access what, but it is not the tool that records API call history.

q_7311ce562ed6.explanation: AWS Service Catalog lets an organization create and govern catalogs of approved IaC templates and manage the IT services deployed from them.

optionNotes.A: Resource Explorer searches and discovers existing resources; it does not govern IaC templates.
optionNotes.B: Service Catalog publishes approved templates as products and governs how deployed IT services are provisioned and managed.
optionNotes.C: Organizations manages multiple accounts and policies; it does not manage a catalog of IaC templates.
optionNotes.D: Systems Manager handles operational tasks on resources, not a governed catalog of IaC templates.

q_c584da768fe8.explanation: Systems Manager Parameter Store can hold configuration data and encrypted values (SecureString) centrally, and standard parameters have no additional charge, making it the most cost-effective choice.

optionNotes.A: Parameter Store stores configuration values and passwords centrally, and standard parameters are free, so it is the cheapest fit.
optionNotes.B: AWS KMS creates and manages encryption keys; it is not a store for configuration data and passwords.
optionNotes.C: AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes; it is not a store for application configuration data or passwords.
optionNotes.D: Amazon S3 is object storage and is not designed as a managed, access-controlled store for passwords and configuration parameters.

q_b1b3b59e4755.explanation: The AWS CLI is a unified tool that lets you interact with many AWS services through one consistent command-line interface.

optionNotes.A: The AWS CLI gives one consistent command-line method to manage and interact with AWS services.
optionNotes.B: Amazon ECS runs and orchestrates containers; it is not a tool for interacting with AWS services in general.
optionNotes.C: Cloud9 is a cloud-based IDE for writing code, not the unified interface to AWS services.
optionNotes.D: AWS VPN provides encrypted network connectivity; it is not a tool for calling AWS services.

q_d2f4ce962043.explanation: AWS CloudTrail records API activity in an AWS account, so users can audit who did what and when.

optionNotes.A: CloudTrail logs API calls and account activity, which is what auditing API activity requires.
optionNotes.B: Inspector assesses workloads for vulnerabilities and does not audit API activity.
optionNotes.C: AWS WAF filters web requests to protect applications; it does not log account API calls.
optionNotes.D: AWS Config tracks resource configuration state and changes, not the API calls themselves.

q_82371b515c4a.explanation: AWS Elastic Beanstalk takes an uploaded application and automatically provisions and manages the needed resources, so the developer does not create them manually.

optionNotes.A: EC2 provides virtual servers, but the developer would have to create and configure the surrounding resources manually.
optionNotes.B: Elastic Beanstalk deploys the application and handles provisioning, load balancing, and scaling automatically.
optionNotes.C: CodeBuild compiles and tests code; it does not deploy and run the application's resources.
optionNotes.D: Amazon Personalize is a machine learning recommendation service, unrelated to deploying applications.

q_65236cd6a3b3.explanation: The AWS Health Dashboard shows the availability and operational status of AWS services and events affecting your account.

optionNotes.A: EventBridge routes events between services; it is not a dashboard for AWS service availability.
optionNotes.B: Service Catalog manages approved products for deployment, not service health information.
optionNotes.C: Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account environment, not service health reporting.
optionNotes.D: The Health Dashboard reports AWS service availability, operational issues, and account-specific events.

q_a1707d5ac158.explanation: AWS CloudFormation templates describe multiple AWS resources and can be reused to deploy the same resources repeatedly.

optionNotes.A: AWS Marketplace is a catalog for buying third-party software, not a tool for templating resources.
optionNotes.B: An AMI is a template for a single EC2 instance's software, not for deploying multiple AWS resources.
optionNotes.C: CloudFormation templates define many resources and can be reused to deploy them again and again.
optionNotes.D: OpsWorks was a configuration management service using Chef or Puppet (now retired), not the template service for multiple AWS resources.

q_689303d0d4ce.explanation: AWS CloudShell is a browser-based shell that is pre-authenticated with your console credentials and launches directly from the Management Console.

optionNotes.A: AWS API is the programmatic interface to services, not a browser-based service launched from the console.
optionNotes.B: Lightsail is a simplified service for virtual servers and web apps, not a pre-authenticated shell.
optionNotes.C: Cloud9 is a cloud-based IDE you set up and open, not a pre-authenticated shell launched from the console.
optionNotes.D: CloudShell opens a browser-based command line already authenticated with the signed-in console user.

q_d0bf546fb3f5.explanation: AWS CloudFormation lets you define and manage infrastructure as code using templates.

optionNotes.A: CodePipeline automates release pipelines; it does not define infrastructure as code.
optionNotes.B: CodeDeploy automates application deployments to compute targets, not infrastructure definition.
optionNotes.C: Direct Connect is a dedicated network connection to AWS, unrelated to IaC.
optionNotes.D: CloudFormation provisions and manages infrastructure from templates, which is IaC.

q_7dd6ff5be757.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk deploys and scales a Node.js application automatically from the uploaded code, so little AWS knowledge is needed.

optionNotes.A: CloudFormation needs you to author templates that define the resources, which requires more AWS knowledge.
optionNotes.B: Elastic Beanstalk supports Node.js and handles provisioning, load balancing, and scaling for you.
optionNotes.C: EC2 requires the user to set up and scale the servers themselves, which demands more knowledge.
optionNotes.D: OpsWorks (now retired) needed configuration management setup with Chef or Puppet, which was more involved than Beanstalk.

q_a178ab2a1f4e.explanation: The AWS CDK lets developers define cloud infrastructure in familiar languages such as TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

optionNotes.A: CodeBuild compiles and tests code; it does not define infrastructure in programming languages.
optionNotes.B: CloudFormation uses JSON or YAML templates rather than general-purpose programming languages.
optionNotes.C: The AWS CLI runs commands from a shell; it is not a framework for defining infrastructure in code languages.
optionNotes.D: The CDK supports TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET and synthesizes the code into CloudFormation templates.

q_5dacc5eb4e1c.explanation: In the AWS CAF platform perspective, data engineering and CI/CD are capabilities. The others belong to the operations and security perspectives.

optionNotes.A: Performance and capacity management is a capability of the operations perspective, not the platform perspective.
optionNotes.B: Data engineering is a capability in the platform perspective.
optionNotes.C: CI/CD is a capability in the platform perspective.
optionNotes.D: Infrastructure protection is a capability of the security perspective.
optionNotes.E: Change and release management is a capability of the operations perspective.

q_ec9f2e45232c.explanation: AWS CloudTrail records API calls such as TerminateInstances, so it shows which action and which user made the EC2 instance inaccessible.

optionNotes.A: CloudWatch Logs holds log data from applications and systems; it does not record account API actions.
optionNotes.B: Security Hub aggregates security findings and does not provide the history of API actions.
optionNotes.C: Inspector assesses vulnerabilities and does not show what action changed an instance.
optionNotes.D: CloudTrail logs the API calls on the account, revealing who or what stopped or terminated the instance.

q_0925c9a0e4cc.explanation: The AWS CLI lets developers provision and manage AWS services through commands that can be put into scripts.

optionNotes.A: The AWS CLI runs commands that can be scripted to create and manage AWS services quickly.
optionNotes.B: CodeBuild compiles and tests code, not a way to script provisioning of services.
optionNotes.C: AWS CAF is guidance for cloud adoption, not a tool for provisioning.
optionNotes.D: Session Manager gives shell access to instances; it is not an offering for scripting AWS service provisioning.

q_ba0c5660dc42.explanation: AWS CloudFormation deploys the same template again and again, so multiple test environments can be created quickly and consistently.

optionNotes.A: EC2 provides servers, but building each environment by hand is neither fast nor repeatable.
optionNotes.B: CloudFormation provisions whole environments from a template in a fast, repeatable way.
optionNotes.C: QuickSight is a business intelligence service, unrelated to deploying environments.
optionNotes.D: ECS runs containers, but it does not itself define and repeat full test environments.

q_900fc170ef5e.explanation: AWS CodePipeline is the AWS continuous delivery service that automates the build, test and deploy phases of a release process, so it meets a CI/CD pipeline requirement. AWS CodeStar, which used to set up such a toolchain quickly, is no longer available.

optionNotes.A: AWS Config evaluates resource configuration and is not a CI/CD service.
optionNotes.B: Cognito handles user sign-up and sign-in, not CI/CD.
optionNotes.C: DataSync transfers data between storage systems, not a CI/CD pipeline.
optionNotes.D: CodePipeline models and automates the release pipeline (source, build, test and deploy) as a continuous delivery service.

q_b3172b72379e.explanation: A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric such as CPU utilization and can trigger an Auto Scaling policy to add or remove instances.

optionNotes.A: SQS is a message queue and does not evaluate CPU utilization to trigger scaling.
optionNotes.B: SNS sends notifications, but it does not itself monitor CPU and start the scaling action.
optionNotes.C: Systems Manager manages operations tasks on instances, not metric-based scaling triggers.
optionNotes.D: A CloudWatch alarm monitors CPU utilization and initiates the Auto Scaling policy when the threshold is crossed.

q_912eae091ab2.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk lets the company deploy applications quickly while it handles provisioning and management of the underlying resources.

optionNotes.A: AWS Config tracks configuration compliance and does not deploy applications.
optionNotes.B: Elastic Beanstalk deploys applications fast and reduces the complexity of managing resources.
optionNotes.C: EC2 requires you to manage servers and related resources yourself, which adds complexity.
optionNotes.D: Amazon Personalize is a recommendation service and has nothing to do with deployment.

q_357cf9a4c7e9.explanation: An AWS SDK lets developers call AWS services from within application code in their chosen programming language.

optionNotes.A: AWS SDKs provide language libraries for accessing AWS services from application code.
optionNotes.B: The Management Console is a web interface for people, not a mechanism for code.
optionNotes.C: CodePipeline automates release workflows; it is not a library for application code.
optionNotes.D: AWS Config tracks resource configurations and does not give code access to services.

q_b447fe78db1e.explanation: An AWS SDK lets application code, such as a web application's backend or browser code, call AWS services programmatically.

optionNotes.A: CloudShell is a browser-based shell for people to run commands, not something a web application uses.
optionNotes.B: AWS Marketplace is a catalog for buying software and does not let an application call AWS services.
optionNotes.C: The Management Console is a web interface for people to manage resources manually, not for application-to-service calls.
optionNotes.D: AWS SDKs are the way application code calls AWS services programmatically.

q_e91a696a76e6.explanation: AWS CloudFormation creates infrastructure from code in the form of templates.

optionNotes.A: EKS runs managed Kubernetes; it is not the IaC service for creating infrastructure from code.
optionNotes.B: Outposts brings AWS infrastructure on premises and is not an IaC tool.
optionNotes.C: CodePipeline automates software release pipelines rather than creating infrastructure from code.
optionNotes.D: CloudFormation provisions infrastructure from code through templates.

q_7f35c0694d02.explanation: AWS Elastic Beanstalk deploys and manages applications in the AWS Cloud without the user handling the underlying infrastructure.

optionNotes.A: CodeGuru provides automated code reviews and performance recommendations, not application deployment.
optionNotes.B: Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers, not a service for deploying and managing applications in general.
optionNotes.C: CodeCommit hosts Git repositories for source code, not deployment.
optionNotes.D: Elastic Beanstalk deploys, scales, and manages applications on AWS.

q_e51804383ea5.explanation: Loosely coupling components means a failure in one component does not cascade to the components that depend on it.

optionNotes.A: A monolithic design ties components together, so failures spread instead of being isolated.
optionNotes.B: Designing for automation reduces manual effort but is not the principle about isolating failures between components.
optionNotes.C: Designing for single points of failure is the opposite of good practice; you should avoid them.
optionNotes.D: Loose coupling isolates failures between dependent components so one failing does not bring down the others.

q_d122ff0c3e43.explanation: Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics and logs from applications and resources, making it easier to monitor and troubleshoot them.

optionNotes.A: EC2 provides compute capacity and is not a monitoring service.
optionNotes.B: IAM manages access permissions and does not monitor logs or resources.
optionNotes.C: CloudWatch gathers logs and metrics for monitoring and troubleshooting applications and resources.
optionNotes.D: CloudTrail records API activity for auditing, not application logs and resource performance.

q_2cd6d9907a47.explanation: Amazon CloudWatch monitors AWS resources and applications in real time through metrics, alarms, and logs.

optionNotes.A: Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks and recommendations, not real-time resource monitoring.
optionNotes.B: CloudWatch collects and tracks metrics and alarms for resources and applications in real time.
optionNotes.C: CloudTrail records API calls for auditing and is not a real-time performance monitor.
optionNotes.D: Cost Explorer analyzes cost and usage, not resource and application health.

q_1ed4d1c36e49.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk accepts the Java application as is and automatically handles capacity provisioning, load balancing, scaling, and health monitoring.

optionNotes.A: ECS orchestrates containers, but the application is non-containerized, so it is not the best fit.
optionNotes.B: Lambda runs functions in response to events and is not a managed platform for deploying a Java web application with load balancing.
optionNotes.C: EKS runs Kubernetes for containerized workloads, which this application is not.
optionNotes.D: Elastic Beanstalk deploys non-containerized Java apps and handles provisioning, load balancing, scaling, and health monitoring.

q_8918b7b0b0a7.explanation: AWS SDKs let users connect to AWS and deploy and manage resources programmatically from code.

optionNotes.A: QuickSight is a business intelligence service, not a tool to deploy resources programmatically.
optionNotes.B: PrivateLink provides private connectivity to services, not programmatic deployment.
optionNotes.C: Direct Connect is a dedicated network link to AWS, not a programmatic access tool.
optionNotes.D: AWS SDKs offer language-specific libraries to call AWS services and deploy resources from code.

q_8c2426d61cbf.explanation: AWS CloudTrail records the API calls made in an AWS account so they can be audited.

optionNotes.A: CloudTrail logs API calls in the account, enabling audits of who did what.
optionNotes.B: Trusted Advisor provides best-practice recommendations rather than API call logs.
optionNotes.C: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities in workloads and does not audit API calls.
optionNotes.D: X-Ray traces requests through an application for debugging, not account API calls.

q_1d828c5383f1.explanation: Loose coupling lets components operate independently so the application stays available when one component fails.

optionNotes.A: Disposable resources means treating servers as replaceable, which does not address isolating component failures.
optionNotes.B: Automation reduces manual work but does not by itself keep the application up when a component fails.
optionNotes.C: Rightsizing matches resources to demand and is about cost and efficiency, not failure tolerance.
optionNotes.D: Loose coupling isolates components so one failure does not take the application down.

q_29fe750f6576.explanation: AWS CodeDeploy automates the release of application changes to compute targets.

optionNotes.A: AppFlow transfers data between SaaS applications and AWS, not application releases.
optionNotes.B: CodeDeploy automates deployments of application changes to EC2, on-premises servers, Lambda, or ECS.
optionNotes.C: PrivateLink offers private network access to services, not a release tool.
optionNotes.D: EKS Distro is a Kubernetes distribution, not a service for automated releases.

q_7596d83ffa02.explanation: CloudTrail records who called which API and when, so it identifies who accessed a service and what they did.

optionNotes.A: CloudWatch monitors metrics and logs, not the identity behind API actions.
optionNotes.B: CloudTrail logs the caller identity, action, and time for activity in the account.
optionNotes.C: Security Hub aggregates security findings and does not log individual API calls.
optionNotes.D: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and does not record user activity.

q_144d82720e24.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk lets developers deploy their applications without provisioning the infrastructure themselves, because it creates and manages it.

optionNotes.A: CloudFormation requires developers to write templates that define the infrastructure.
optionNotes.B: CodeBuild compiles and tests source code; it does not provision or deploy infrastructure.
optionNotes.C: Elastic Beanstalk takes the application code and provisions the infrastructure automatically.
optionNotes.D: CodeDeploy deploys application revisions to existing targets and does not provision infrastructure.

q_a871f520588b.explanation: AWS Config records resource configurations and compliance over time, producing information that external auditors can use.

optionNotes.A: Cognito manages user identity and authentication, not audit information.
optionNotes.B: FSx provides managed file systems and is not an audit service.
optionNotes.C: AWS Config records configuration history and compliance evaluations that auditors can review.
optionNotes.D: Amazon Polly converts text to speech and does not produce audit information.

q_3ed64d52376b.explanation: AWS CloudFormation deploys the same infrastructure configuration repeatedly from a template.

optionNotes.A: CloudFormation uses templates to deploy highly repeatable infrastructure configurations.
optionNotes.B: CodeDeploy deploys application code, not infrastructure configurations.
optionNotes.C: CodeBuild builds and tests source code and does not deploy infrastructure.
optionNotes.D: Systems Manager handles operational tasks on resources, not repeatable infrastructure templates.

q_4a3cba64b767.explanation: Amazon EventBridge receives events such as EC2 state changes and can route them to a target like a Lambda function.

optionNotes.A: EventBridge matches the EC2 instance state-change event with a rule and invokes the Lambda function.
optionNotes.B: AWS Config tracks configuration changes and compliance, and is not the usual way to trigger a function on a state change.
optionNotes.C: SNS delivers notifications to subscribers; it is not the service that detects the EC2 state-change event.
optionNotes.D: CloudFormation provisions resources and does not react to EC2 state changes.

q_97736b328a7f.explanation: AWS CloudTrail records account activity and API calls, supporting governance, compliance, and risk auditing.

optionNotes.A: MFA adds an extra sign-in factor and is not an auditing feature.
optionNotes.B: Lambda runs code without servers and does not audit accounts.
optionNotes.C: SNS sends notifications and does not record activity for auditing.
optionNotes.D: CloudTrail logs account activity that supports governance, compliance, and risk auditing.

q_626b0755738a.explanation: CloudTrail records actions taken in the account, which supports the design principle of activating traceability.

optionNotes.A: Activating traceability means logging and monitoring actions, which is what CloudTrail does.
optionNotes.B: Using serverless compute architectures relates to services like Lambda, not CloudTrail.
optionNotes.C: Performing operations as code relates to tools like CloudFormation, not logging activity.
optionNotes.D: Going global in minutes relates to deploying in multiple Regions, not to CloudTrail.

q_94032daa8514.explanation: The AWS CDK is a development framework for defining cloud resources in code and provisioning them through CloudFormation.

optionNotes.A: The AWS CLI runs commands to interact with services and is not a framework that generates CloudFormation.
optionNotes.B: The AWS Developer Center is a resource site for developers, not a framework.
optionNotes.C: The CDK lets you define resources in programming languages and deploys them through CloudFormation.
optionNotes.D: CodeStar set up development projects and toolchains (and has since been discontinued), but it is not the framework for defining resources as code.

q_566013175508.explanation: AWS Service Catalog lets organizations manage approved IaC templates as products, helping meet compliance requirements.

optionNotes.A: Artifact provides compliance reports and agreements, not management of IaC templates.
optionNotes.B: Resource Explorer finds resources and does not manage IaC templates.
optionNotes.C: License Manager tracks software licenses, not IaC templates.
optionNotes.D: Service Catalog manages approved IaC templates so deployments follow compliance requirements.

q_77dcf3d5cb74.explanation: Amazon CloudWatch collects EC2 metrics such as CPU utilization.

optionNotes.A: AWS Config tracks configuration changes, not performance metrics like CPU.
optionNotes.B: Trusted Advisor provides best-practice recommendations, not detailed CPU utilization monitoring.
optionNotes.C: CloudTrail records API activity and not resource performance.
optionNotes.D: CloudWatch provides CPU utilization metrics for EC2 instances.

q_a79a4b607893.explanation: AWS CloudFormation lets a company define and provision infrastructure as code with templates.

optionNotes.A: CodeDeploy deploys applications, not infrastructure defined as code.
optionNotes.B: Elastic Beanstalk deploys applications and manages their environment, but it is not the service for treating infrastructure as code.
optionNotes.C: API Gateway creates and publishes APIs and is unrelated to infrastructure as code.
optionNotes.D: CloudFormation provisions infrastructure from templates, which is the IaC approach.

q_98e137023d33.explanation: CloudTrail records who initiated an event and which actions were performed, which fits an audit of recent account activity.

optionNotes.A: AWS Config records resource configuration changes, not the identity and API actions behind an event.
optionNotes.B: Rekognition analyzes images and video and has nothing to do with account auditing.
optionNotes.C: CloudTrail records the user and the actions performed in the account.
optionNotes.D: SNS sends notifications and does not log account activity.

q_002a9372a1a1.explanation: The AWS Health Dashboard publishes service status that users can follow, including through RSS feeds, for AWS service issues.

optionNotes.A: SNS delivers messages to subscribers but is not the source of the RSS feeds about AWS service issues.
optionNotes.B: The Health Dashboard shows AWS service issues and offers RSS feeds for updates.
optionNotes.C: AWS Config records resource configuration and is unrelated to service issue feeds.
optionNotes.D: CodeCommit hosts source code repositories, not service status feeds.

q_29f0d437d9c8.explanation: AWS Control Tower sets up and governs a secure multi-account AWS environment based on best practices.

optionNotes.A: CloudFormation provisions resources from templates, but does not set up and govern a multi-account environment by itself.
optionNotes.B: Control Tower automates setting up a multi-account landing zone with governance guardrails.
optionNotes.C: AWS Config evaluates resource configurations and is not used to set up a multi-account environment.
optionNotes.D: Amazon VPC provides a virtual network and does not set up a multi-account environment.

q_68d76e247354.explanation: The AWS CDK supports Python and TypeScript among its languages, while Swift, Ruby, and PHP are not supported.

optionNotes.A: Python is a language supported by the AWS CDK.
optionNotes.B: Swift is not a supported CDK language.
optionNotes.C: TypeScript is a language supported by the AWS CDK.
optionNotes.D: Ruby is not a supported CDK language.
optionNotes.E: PHP is not a supported CDK language.

q_8ffbed89e394.explanation: The AWS CDK lets users provision AWS infrastructure programmatically by defining it in code.

optionNotes.A: The CDK defines infrastructure in programming languages and provisions it through CloudFormation.
optionNotes.B: CodeGuru gives code review and performance recommendations, not infrastructure provisioning.
optionNotes.C: AWS Config assesses and records resource configuration; it does not provision infrastructure.
optionNotes.D: CodeCommit stores source code in Git repositories and does not provision infrastructure.

q_b08179beaa4e.explanation: CloudFormation templates automate resource creation, which reduces provisioning time and manual effort.

optionNotes.A: Templates automate provisioning of resources, which shortens the time to deploy.
optionNotes.B: Templates do not transfer existing infrastructure to another company.
optionNotes.C: Templates create AWS resources and do not reuse on-premises infrastructure in the cloud.
optionNotes.D: Resources created from templates still incur normal AWS charges, so cost is not eliminated.

q_8a83ad20c364.explanation: CloudTrail keeps an event history of API calls, including those that created resources.

optionNotes.A: CloudWatch collects metrics and logs but does not record an event history of resource creation.
optionNotes.B: CloudTrail provides the event history of API activity, including resource creation.
optionNotes.C: Amazon Aurora is a relational database service and not a source of account event history.
optionNotes.D: EventBridge routes events to targets and is not the record of past resource creation.

q_baa5e508c05c.explanation: CloudFormation can deploy the same template to multiple Regions (for example with StackSets), creating copies of resources across Regions.

optionNotes.A: Amazon Cognito provides user sign-up, sign-in and access control for applications; it does not create copies of resources across Regions.
optionNotes.B: CloudFormation deploys the same template in multiple Regions to create copies of resources.
optionNotes.C: CloudTrail logs API activity and does not create resources.
optionNotes.D: Systems Manager manages operational tasks on resources; deploying the same set of resources to several Regions is CloudFormation's role.

q_c3be02bc64cf.explanation: Amazon CloudWatch collects EC2 metrics such as disk write operations and can alarm on spikes.

optionNotes.A: CloudTrail logs API calls, not disk performance metrics.
optionNotes.B: The Health Dashboard shows AWS service health, not performance of your own instance disks.
optionNotes.C: Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations and does not monitor disk write activity.
optionNotes.D: CloudWatch monitors metrics like disk writes and can raise alarms when they spike.

q_be5053cc8134.explanation: CloudTrail records the TerminateInstances API call, showing when an EC2 instance was terminated.

optionNotes.A: IAM manages permissions and does not keep a history of terminated instances.
optionNotes.B: CloudTrail logs the API call that terminated the instance, including the time.
optionNotes.C: Compute Optimizer recommends instance sizes and does not record terminations.
optionNotes.D: Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video; it does not record EC2 instance events.

q_b3802c5eaf59.explanation: AWS Config records configuration changes, evaluates them against rules, and can remediate noncompliant resources.

optionNotes.A: AWS Config records and evaluates configuration changes and supports remediation actions.
optionNotes.B: Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets and does not track configuration compliance.
optionNotes.C: CloudTrail records API calls but does not evaluate configuration compliance or remediate.
optionNotes.D: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations but does not record configuration history or remediate changes.

q_41f4d02ba0bc.explanation: CloudFormation uses a standardized template to create copies of the same architecture for development, test, and production.

optionNotes.A: Cloud Map is a service discovery tool and does not create architecture from templates.
optionNotes.B: CloudFormation creates consistent copies of an architecture from one template.
optionNotes.C: CloudFront is a content delivery network and does not create environments.
optionNotes.D: CloudTrail logs API calls and does not provision architecture.

q_f6845f930a58.explanation: The AWS Management Console provides a graphical web interface for managing AWS services.

optionNotes.A: AWS Copilot is a command-line tool for containerized apps, not a graphical interface.
optionNotes.B: The AWS CLI is command-line based, not graphical.
optionNotes.C: The Management Console is the graphical web interface for managing AWS services.
optionNotes.D: SDKs are libraries used in code, not a graphical interface.

q_9945ee071a0a.explanation: CodeDeploy automates software deployments to EC2 instances and on-premises servers.

optionNotes.A: CodeCommit hosts source code repositories and does not deploy software.
optionNotes.B: CodeBuild compiles and tests code; deploying software to instances is CodeDeploy's job.
optionNotes.C: CodeDeploy automates deployments to both EC2 and on-premises instances.
optionNotes.D: CodePipeline orchestrates the release workflow and can include deploy actions, but CodeDeploy is the service dedicated to deploying to EC2 and on-premises instances.

q_9a47c2ac7d1e.explanation: CloudTrail logs deletion API calls with the identity of the user, so it shows who deleted the resources.

optionNotes.A: CloudTrail records API calls and the user who made them, identifying who deleted resources.
optionNotes.B: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and does not record deletions.
optionNotes.C: GuardDuty detects threats and anomalies but is not the record of which user deleted resources.
optionNotes.D: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations and does not show who deleted resources.

q_df961a688edf.explanation: The AWS Management Console is the web interface for managing AWS resources.

optionNotes.A: The Management Console is the web-based interface for managing AWS resources.
optionNotes.B: The AWS CLI is a command-line tool and not a web interface.
optionNotes.C: SDKs are code libraries and not a web interface.
optionNotes.D: Cloud9 is a cloud IDE for writing code, not the general web interface to manage resources.

q_fda2759e876f.explanation: CloudFormation templates let a developer create and maintain development and production infrastructure repeatably.

optionNotes.A: Ground Station is for satellite communications and is unrelated to environments.
optionNotes.B: AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks and does not provision infrastructure.
optionNotes.C: IoT Device Defender audits IoT device security and does not provision environments.
optionNotes.D: CloudFormation builds the same infrastructure repeatedly from templates.

auth-deploy-operate-01.explanation: By default CloudFormation rolls back the stack when a resource fails to create, deleting the resources it already created.

optionNotes.A: A failed creation does not leave the stack marked complete; the stack goes into rollback.
optionNotes.B: Rollback on failure is the default behavior and it removes the resources created so far, returning to a clean state.
optionNotes.C: CloudFormation does not retry a failed resource in another Region.
optionNotes.D: CloudFormation does not convert templates into CDK code on failure.

auth-deploy-operate-02.explanation: CloudTrail records the API call that changed the security group rule, including the IAM user and the time.

optionNotes.A: CloudWatch monitors metrics and logs, not the identity behind a configuration change.
optionNotes.B: The Health Dashboard reports AWS service events, not who changed your resources.
optionNotes.C: X-Ray traces application requests and does not record management API calls.
optionNotes.D: CloudTrail logs the API call with the caller identity and timestamp.

auth-deploy-operate-03.explanation: CloudWatch can trigger alarm actions such as stopping an idle EC2 instance, and it collects and searches logs with CloudWatch Logs.

optionNotes.A: A CloudWatch alarm on low CPU can perform an action that stops the instance.
optionNotes.B: Rotating IAM access keys automatically is not a CloudWatch task.
optionNotes.C: CloudWatch Logs collects and searches logs from applications and AWS services.
optionNotes.D: Evaluating configuration compliance over time is a task for AWS Config.
optionNotes.E: Accepting agreements such as a BAA is done in AWS Artifact.

auth-deploy-operate-04.explanation: AWS Config continuously evaluates resources against rules such as encrypted volumes and keeps configuration history over time.

optionNotes.A: CodePipeline automates release pipelines and does not evaluate resource compliance.
optionNotes.B: EventBridge Scheduler runs scheduled tasks and does not check configuration compliance or keep history.
optionNotes.C: AWS Config checks resources against rules continuously and tracks configuration changes over time.
optionNotes.D: CloudShell is a browser-based shell and not a compliance tool.

auth-deploy-operate-05.explanation: Session Manager gives browser or CLI shell access to instances without inbound SSH ports, bastion hosts, or SSH keys.

optionNotes.A: Session Manager connects to instances without opening inbound ports, using bastions, or managing SSH keys.
optionNotes.B: CloudFormation change sets preview stack updates and do not provide instance access.
optionNotes.C: CloudWatch dashboards display metrics and do not provide shell access.
optionNotes.D: CodeDeploy deploys software and does not provide administrative access to instances.

auth-deploy-operate-06.explanation: Blue/green deployment keeps the old environment running while the new one is tested, allowing a quick switch back.

optionNotes.A: All at once in place updates every instance together and removes the old version, so a quick return is hard.
optionNotes.B: Blue/green runs old and new environments side by side, allowing rapid rollback by switching traffic back.
optionNotes.C: Rolling in place replaces instances gradually and does not keep the full old environment running.
optionNotes.D: Redeploying from backups is slow and does not allow a switch back within seconds.

auth-deploy-operate-07.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk provisions capacity, load balancing, and scaling for an uploaded application, and developers keep control over the underlying resources. There is no extra charge for Beanstalk itself.

optionNotes.A: Beanstalk handles provisioning, load balancing, and auto scaling for the application you upload.
optionNotes.B: There is no additional charge for Beanstalk; you pay only for the underlying resources it uses.
optionNotes.C: Beanstalk supports many platforms such as Java, .NET, Node.js, and Python, as well as Docker, not only containers.
optionNotes.D: Developers retain control of the AWS resources that run the application and can adjust them.
optionNotes.E: Recording API calls for auditing is the job of CloudTrail, not Beanstalk.

auth-deploy-operate-08.explanation: The AWS Health Dashboard shows service events affecting your resources and scheduled maintenance such as instance retirements.

optionNotes.A: AWS Config tracks resource configuration and compliance, not AWS service issues or maintenance events.
optionNotes.B: CloudWatch Logs stores log data and does not report AWS service events for your account.
optionNotes.C: CodePipeline automates deployments and does not report service issues.
optionNotes.D: The Health Dashboard reports ongoing service issues and scheduled maintenance affecting your account.

auth-deploy-operate-09.explanation: AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed build service that compiles code and runs unit tests without managing build servers.

optionNotes.A: CodeDeploy deploys applications and does not compile or test code.
optionNotes.B: Elastic Beanstalk deploys and runs applications, not managed builds.
optionNotes.C: CodeBuild compiles source code and runs tests without servers to provision or patch.
optionNotes.D: Patch Manager patches managed nodes and is not a build service.

auth-deploy-operate-10.explanation: CloudFormation provisions the same infrastructure repeatably across Regions or accounts and manages related resources together as a stack.

optionNotes.A: Patching guest operating systems is done by tools like Systems Manager Patch Manager, not CloudFormation.
optionNotes.B: The same template can be deployed repeatedly across Regions and accounts.
optionNotes.C: Alerts on CPU thresholds come from CloudWatch alarms, not CloudFormation.
optionNotes.D: Recording configuration history for compliance is the role of AWS Config.
optionNotes.E: A stack groups related resources so they can be created or deleted as a unit.
